title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying the preregistered guarded exclusion policy changes validator‑based success rates. Execution used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") under shared generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one shared generation per item. All 150 baseline and matched guarded episodes passed the deterministic validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Critically, and as recorded in the archived artifacts, the primary confirmatory estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) became degenerate/untestable under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and provenance‑stable synthetic sampling; this paper explicitly documents that preregistered public‑benchmark targets were not sampled and explains, using artifact references, why the run was insensitive to generation‑level contamination and how audit designs should be modified to regain sensitivity.

sections.introduction: LLMs are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated repair. Operational adoption requires trustworthy evaluations: measured success must reflect model capability rather than dataset contamination or templated leakage. We preregistered an oracle‑backed paired audit (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) to test whether conservative deterministic detectors and a guarded exclusion policy materially change validator pass rates on a reproducible 150‑item sample. The preregistration targeted four public NetOps benchmark identifiers (OpenAlex IDs): https://openalex.org/W7157506260, https://openalex.org/W4404602270, https://openalex.org/W4404534210, and https://openalex.org/W7166900660 and is recorded by the preregistration SHA‑256 = 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a (preregistration present in the archived execution bundle). After execution we observed zero high‑confidence contamination flags and exact concordance across paired episodes. This paper (1) reports the exact artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics for Npairs = 150; (2) documents an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation with concrete artifact pointers and hashes that explain why the run produced a degenerate null; and (3) provides artifact‑anchored recommendations to make future audits sensitive to web‑sourced contamination. We emphasize scope: the reported null applies to the executed synthetic, shared‑generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks.
sections.related_work: Empirical and systems work show LLMs can translate intent into device configurations and propose repairs; integrating validators and iterative validate–repair loops typically improves average repair quality (see recent benchmarks and system papers). Formal verification tools and header‑space analyses serve as practical oracles for reachability and policy checks and are commonly used in generate–validate pipelines. Parallel literature on evaluation validity highlights contamination and construct‑validity risks (hallucination, templating, leakage) and prescribes fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance tracing, and pre‑registered defenses. Our audit sits at the intersection: implementing conservative, preregistered detectors and an oracle validator in a fully archived pipeline and then diagnosing, with artifact pointers, why the chosen execution semantics rendered the primary paired contrast uninformative for contamination detection in this run.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. We froze the confirmatory plan (study_id contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a8747a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a) which specified: paired design (baseline vs guarded), 150 items sampled, conservative detectors (exact token equality; 5‑gram fuzzy overlap with high‑confidence threshold ≥0.80), a guarded policy that excludes only high‑confidence flags and replaces them deterministically, and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline analyzed by an exact McNemar two‑sided test plus paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Planned maximum_model_calls = 300 (two independent generations per item) was recorded in the preregistration.

Detectors, validator, and replacement rules. The detection suite implemented (1) exact normalized token equality, (2) 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥0.80 and lower sensitivity brackets at 0.65/0.50 for secondary analyses, and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics to flag items predating a model training cutoff. The oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) which parses candidate configs, simulates state updates against the task's device model, and enforces required_final_state and workflow constraints; it emits binary pass/fail with detailed traces. The guarded policy deterministically excluded only high‑confidence flagged items and replaced them via deterministic retemplating and topology augmentation subject to an embedding similarity safeguard (cosine ≥ 0.85). These components and rules were implemented and archived in the execution bundle; representative artifacts include execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini", independent_condition_generation = false) with SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820 and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (deterministic generator seeds and task_payloads) with SHA‑256 = b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55.

Generation semantics and preregistration→execution choices. The preregistration allowed either independent_condition_generation or shared generation semantics but planned two independent generations per item (max 300 model calls) for best sensitivity. The executed run set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics), recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA above). Under this semantics the pipeline performed a single model generation per item and reused it for both baseline and guarded episodes unless an exclusion/replacement occurred; provider accounting shows model_calls_used = 150 and completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 150 (execution manifest). This single‑call choice mechanically reduces observable discordance and thus the capacity to detect generation‑level differences arising from contamination.

Logging and persisted artifacts. The detector implementation persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only when a threshold crossing or replacement occurred (an implementation detail consistent with the preregistered artifact‑persistence policy). Because no items met the preregistered high‑confidence threshold in this execution, the detector did not persist a global per‑item overlap table; this is evidenced by analysis/contamination_summary.csv (empty) with SHA‑256 = 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222 and execution/raw_results.jsonl with SHA‑256 = 5337998d1d86aca507f77659d75cc9487cf3d87a157ed5044b8a9d5ff79b5586. The absence of a persisted global overlap distribution is an explicit, artifact‑documented consequence of the implemented persistence policy and the observed absence of threshold crossings.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The archived execution manifest records: planned_episode_count = 300, completed_episode_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item) (see execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e2... and execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = b7c08599...). The deterministic validator produced passes for all episodes: baseline_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_count = 150/150. The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e). The primary estimand (guarded − baseline) = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode raw responses and validator traces are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 5337998d...).

Representative diagnostic episode. A representative archived episode (pair‑000001 / task‑000001) shows identical normalized_reference_answer and normalized_response: "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up"; validator parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION). The full validator trace for this episode is stored under execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (artifact examples in the bundle) and supports the interpretation that the validator checks were applied as preregistered.

Contamination detection outcome and missing overlap table. The preregistered high‑confidence detector produced zero flags for the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (SHA‑256 = 389227f0...). Because the detector persisted per‑item fuzzy overlap scores only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred, no global per‑item overlap distribution artifact was produced. This is an explicit, artifact‑grounded absence—not an unlogged omission—and it limits post‑hoc inspection of how close items were to the preregistered thresholds. The implications are discussed below.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand was degenerate (artifact‑anchored diagnosis). Two execution facts recorded in the archived artifacts jointly explain the observed complete concordance: (1) the sampled items in this run were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (each manifest entry contains source_identifier starting with "synthetic-netops:"); and (2) the pipeline executed with shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e2...). With one shared generation per item and no high‑confidence exclusions, baseline and guarded episodes are identical by construction and the paired contrast cannot reveal contamination effects that would manifest only under independent regeneration or on web‑sourced items. We therefore unambiguously reclassify the primary confirmatory estimand as degenerate/untestable under the executed semantics: the p = 1.0 and CI = [0,0] correctly summarize the executed data but do not support inference about contamination prevalence in web‑sourced benchmarks.

Concrete remedial design changes (artifact‑anchored). To make future audits sensitive to web‑sourced contamination the archived artifacts support these recommended changes (implementable within the same pipeline): (A) sample provenance‑rich public items (use the preregistered benchmark_scope OpenAlex IDs) rather than synthetic generator outputs; (B) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded episodes are independently realized and discordant pairs can arise; (C) persist per‑item fuzzy overlap scores unconditionally (produce analysis/contamination_scores.csv for every run) so threshold sensitivity can be assessed; (D) increase independent draws (multi‑model or multiple seeds) to raise power for modest effect sizes; and (E) add paraphrase‑sensitive detectors plus human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from the recorded gaps: model_calls_used = 150 (execution manifest), empty contamination_summary.csv (analysis artifact), and lack of per‑item overlap distribution in the archive.

Threats to validity and operational implications. Internal validity: generation semantics and shared caching collapsed independent trials; prompt sensitivity remains possible. Construct validity: conservative lexical detectors can miss paraphrased leakage; validators check preregistered functional constraints but not every operational harm. External validity: single‑model execution (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic sampling limit generalization to other LLM families and web‑sourced benchmarks. Conclusion validity: the degenerate paired outcome arises from execution choices, not an empirical confirmation of absence of contamination in external datasets. Therefore, operational audit claims must combine provenance‑rich sampling, independent generations, cross‑model checks, and human adjudication.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, archived paired audit of conservative contamination detectors in an LLM‑for‑NetOps pipeline. Artifact‑verified results show zero preregistered high‑confidence flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The run's primary contrast was degenerate and uninformative for web‑sourced contamination due to execution choices that are themselves recorded in the archive—specifically, provenance‑stable synthetic sampling (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55) and shared_initial_candidate generation (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). We (a) make that reclassification explicit, (b) provide the artifact‑anchored reconciliation required to verify the execution→preregistration divergence (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a8747a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a), and (c) recommend concrete, implementable changes to restore audit sensitivity for public benchmarks. All raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts cited above are archived in the execution bundle and may be re‑run with modified generation semantics to perform a non‑degenerate contamination audit that targets the preregistered public benchmark identifiers listed above.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items in this execution were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"); absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in web‑crawled public benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to the preregistered intervention.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

Passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
